title: Looking up in constant time
objectives: Replace a nested loop with a hash map.

screens.title: A bucket for every key
screens.prose: A toy rule picks a bucket for each ticker. Add the letters' places in the alphabet (A = 1, B = 2, up to Z = 26). Then keep the remainder after dividing by 5.

state.caption: Bucket = (sum of letter places) mod 5. AB is $1 + 2 = 3$: bucket 3.

screens.question: Drag each ticker into its bucket.

hints.text: Work out each ticker's letter sum first.
For VOD: V = 22, O = 15, D = 4.
VOD: 41 leaves 1, so bucket 1. BP: 18 leaves 3. HSBA: 30 leaves 0.

feedback.correct: VOD in bucket 1, BP in bucket 3, HSBA in bucket 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the letter places, divide by 5, and use the remainder.

byKey.vod: VOD is $22 + 15 + 4 = 41$, and 41 leaves 1 after dividing by 5: bucket 1.
byKey.bp: BP is $2 + 16 = 18$, which leaves 3 after dividing by 5: bucket 3.
byKey.hsba: HSBA is $8 + 19 + 2 + 1 = 30$, which divides exactly by 5: bucket 0.

explain.text: The rule turns each key into a bucket number with one short sum. To find VOD later, we redo the sum and look in bucket 1 alone. That rule is a **hash function**, and the buckets make a **hash table**.

screens.title: A crowded bucket
screens.prose: The three tickers are stored. Now AZN arrives, with the same rule: letter places added, remainder after dividing by 5.
screens.question: Drag AZN into its bucket.

hints.text: $1 + 26 + 14 = 41$. Which ticker also had 41?
41 leaves 1, so AZN joins VOD in bucket 1.

feedback.correct: AZN lands in bucket 1, next to VOD.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out AZN's letter sum and its remainder after dividing by 5.

byKey.azn: AZN is $1 + 26 + 14 = 41$, the same sum as VOD. It goes in bucket 1 too, even though that bucket is taken.
byKey.vod: VOD was already in the right bucket. Leave it there.
byKey.bp: BP was already in the right bucket. Leave it there.
byKey.hsba: HSBA was already in the right bucket. Leave it there.

explain.text: AZN and VOD share bucket 1. Two keys in one bucket is a **collision**. The bucket keeps both, and a lookup compares the keys inside it.

canvas.caption: A collision: VOD and AZN both hash to bucket 1

screens.title: Looking AZN up
screens.prose: To look up AZN, Python hashes it to bucket 1. Then it compares AZN with each key there, in arrival order.

state.caption: Four tickers stored. VOD went into bucket 1 first.

screens.question: How many key comparisons does finding AZN take?

hints.text: Which buckets does the lookup visit?
Only bucket 1 is searched.
Bucket 1 holds VOD, then AZN: two comparisons.

feedback.correct: Two comparisons, and the other buckets are never touched.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The hash picks one bucket; count the keys checked inside it.

byKey.every-key: You compared AZN with every ticker in the table. The hash sends the lookup straight to bucket 1, so only VOD and AZN are checked.
byKey.one: The hash finds the bucket in one step, but VOD is there first. AZN is the second key compared.

explain.text: Only bucket 1 is searched: VOD, then AZN. When each bucket holds only a few keys, lookup, insert and delete cost $O(1)$ **on average**, however big the table. Python's dict resolves collisions by probing other slots, but the cost works the same way.

canvas.caption: One hash, one bucket, two comparisons

screens.title: Every key in one bucket
screens.prose: Four new tickers, and by bad luck every one lands in bucket 2. Imagine the same with $n$ keys.

state.caption: GSK 37, RIO 42, TSCO 57, BT 22: all leave 2

screens.question: If all $n$ keys land in one bucket, what does a lookup cost?

options.text: $O(n)$: it compares the key with each one in the bucket

options.why: You trusted the average. With every key in one bucket, the lookup compares against all of them.

options.text: $O(\log n)$: it halves the bucket each time
options.why: The bucket is not sorted, so nothing can be halved. Each key is checked in turn.
One lookup checks each key once. $O(n^2)$ would be $n$ lookups like this one.

hints.text: Find BT. Which keys does the lookup check?
Bucket 2 holds every key.
GSK, RIO, TSCO, then BT: every key, so $O(n)$.

feedback.correct: All keys in one bucket turns the table back into a list.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the comparisons to find the last key in the bucket.

byKey.o1: Hashing finds the bucket in $O(1)$, but then every key in it is compared. Here that is all $n$.

explain.text: A lookup for BT checks GSK, RIO, TSCO and then BT: every key. Real hash functions spread keys evenly, so this is rare. The $O(1)$ is an average, not a promise.

canvas.caption: Worst case: one bucket holds everything, so a lookup is $O(n)$

screens.title: Held in both
screens.question: Each portfolio holds 10,000 tickers. How many `x == y` comparisons run?

hints.text: How many times does the inner loop run for one `x`?
The inner loop runs in full, 10,000 times, for every `x`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The inner loop runs completely for each `x`.

byKey.added: You added the lengths. The inner loop runs in full for every `x`: $10{,}000 \times 10{,}000$.
byKey.one-list: That is one pass over `a`. Each `x` also walks the whole of `b`.
byKey.half: Nothing stops the inner loop early, so every pair is compared. There is no halving here.

explain.text: Every $x$ meets every $y$: $10{,}000 \times 10{,}000 = 10^8$ comparisons. Build `b_set = set(b)` once and test `x in b_set` instead. That is 10,000 inserts and 10,000 lookups, about 20,000 steps.

canvas.caption: Hash `b` once, then each `x` is one lookup

screens.title: A hidden loop
screens.question: A day has 2,000,000 distinct trade ids. About how many comparisons does `i not in seen` make in total?

options.why: You counted `not in` as one step. On a list it compares `i` with every id in `seen`, which grows to 2,000,000.
That is $n \log_2 n$, the cost of sorting. A list scan has no halving; it checks each id in turn.
That is $n^2$. `seen` grows from empty, so the scans average half its final length.

hints.text: What does `i not in seen` do when `seen` is a list?
It compares `i` with each id already in `seen`.
With all ids distinct, the scans are $0 + 1 + \dots + (n - 1) \approx n^2 / 2$.

feedback.correct: About two trillion comparisons: the line that looks like one step is a loop.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `in` on a list checks the items one by one.

byKey.one-step: You treated `i not in seen` as one step. On a list it is a loop over everything seen so far.
byKey.sorting: You used the cost of sorting. Nothing here halves the search: each check walks the list.

explain.text: Each `in` on a list is a hidden loop over `seen`, so the total is about $n^2 / 2 = 2 \times 10^{12}$. Keep a set for the checks and a list for the output. Each check is then $O(1)$ on average: about $2 \times 10^6$ steps.

canvas.caption: Fix: `seen = set()` for the checks, `out = []` for the order

screens.title: What can be a key
screens.prose: A key's hash must never change. Otherwise a lookup would hash it to a different bucket and miss it. So Python lets a value be a key only if it is **hashable**: in practice, if it cannot change.
screens.question: Which of these can be dict keys? Select all that apply.

options.why: A list can change after it is stored, so it has no hash. As a key it raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`.
A dict can change too, so it has no hash and cannot be a key.

hints.text: Which of these could change after it is stored?
Lists and dicts can be changed in place.
Strings, numbers and tuples of them cannot change, so they can be keys.

feedback.correct: Strings, numbers and tuples of them are keys; lists and dicts are not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the values that can never change.

byKey.list: You picked the list. Lists can change, so Python refuses to hash them. The tuple `("VOD", "BP")` works instead.
byKey.dict: You picked the dict. A dict can change, so it has no hash either.

explain.text: Strings, numbers and tuples of them never change, so their hash is fixed. Lists and dicts can change, so they have no hash, and using one as a key raises `TypeError`. A tuple such as `(ticker, date)` is the usual fix.

screens.title: Hash once, look up often
screens.prose:
We replaced a scan with a hash lookup. The pattern:

```python
# O(n * m): a list scan inside a loop
for x in a:
    if x in b_list: ...

# O(n + m): hash once, then O(1) checks
b_set = set(b_list)
for x in a:
    if x in b_set: ...
```

`set`, `dict` and `collections.Counter` all hash their keys.
screens.question: What does building `b_set = set(b_list)` cost, for $m$ items?

options.why: The set must hash every one of the $m$ items, once each.
Each insert is $O(1)$ on average, so $m$ inserts are $O(m)$.
We pay it once, before the loop. Each lookup after that is $O(1)$ on average.

feedback.correct: One pass to build, then cheap checks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many items does the set hash, and how often?

explain.text: Building the set hashes each of the $m$ items once: $O(m)$. The loop then makes $n$ checks at $O(1)$ each. In all, $O(n + m)$ replaces $O(nm)$.

screens.title: Repeated tickers
screens.prose: A position file should list each ticker once. Find the tickers that appear more than once, in a single pass.
screens.question: Write `duplicates(tickers)`: return the tickers that appear more than once, as a sorted list.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests and compares lists exactly, so return the repeats sorted. Tests 7 and 8 use 60,000 and 100,000 tickers: a list scan inside the loop runs out of time.

hints.text: Keep a set of the tickers seen so far.
When a ticker is already in `seen`, it is a repeat.
If `t in seen`, add `t` to `dups`; else add it to `seen`. Return `sorted(dups)`.

feedback.correct: One pass, two sets, and a sorted answer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `['BP', 'VOD']`: each repeat once, sorted. Collect repeats in a set, then return `sorted(...)`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has BARC three times and expects it once. A set of repeats stores it once, however often it recurs.
byKey.error: If the run stopped at the time limit, `seen` is probably a list. Make it a set, so each check is $O(1)$.

explain.text: Each ticker costs one set check and one set insert, $O(1)$ on average, so the pass is $O(n)$. `dups` is a set, so VOD's third copy adds nothing new. Sorting the repeats makes the answer the same on every run.

screens.title: Sector for a million rows
screens.question: If every ticker is equally likely, about how many comparisons does the scan make in total?

hints.text: The `break` stops the scan at the match. Where is the match, on average?
Each of the 500 positions is equally likely, so on average the match is half way.
$\tfrac{1 + 500}{2} = 250.5$ comparisons per row, times 1,000,000 rows.

feedback.correct: About 250 million, against about a million with a dict.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the comparisons for one row, then multiply by the rows.

byKey.full-scan: That is a full scan per row. The `break` stops at the match, which is half way on average.
byKey.dict: That is the dict version: one lookup per row. The scan compares many tickers per row.

explain.text: On average the match is half way down the list: about 250 comparisons per row, 250 million in all. `sector_of = dict(ref)` costs 500 inserts once. Then each row is one $O(1)$ lookup, `sector_of[row.ticker]`: about a million steps.

canvas.caption: `sector_of = dict(ref)`: hash once, look up a million times

ideas: A hash function turns a key into a bucket number, so a lookup goes straight to one bucket. Lookup, insert and delete are $O(1)$ on average.
A scan inside a loop is $O(nm)$. Hash one side into a set or dict first, and the loop becomes $O(n + m)$.
Keys must be hashable: strings, numbers and tuples of them, not lists or dicts. If every key collides, a lookup degrades to $O(n)$.

formula.name: Hash once, then look up
formula.note: Build `set(b)` once, $O(m)$; then $n$ lookups at $O(1)$ each on average.

summary.trap: `if x in seen:` looks like one step. When `seen` is a list it is a loop, and inside another loop it makes the whole thing $O(n^2)$.

options.why: Square brackets never return `None` for a missing key. `d.get("VOD")` does.
`IndexError` is for a list position past the end. A dict is looked up by key.
A plain dict has no default value. `collections.Counter` returns 0 for a missing key.

feedback.correct: A missing key raises `KeyError`, even in an empty dict.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does a dict do when the key is not there?

explain.text: The empty dict has no keys at all, so `d["VOD"]` raises `KeyError`. `d.get("VOD")` returns `None`, and `d.get("VOD", 0)` returns 0.

options.text: It stores the pair as a key
options.why: You expected any value to work as a key. A list can change, so it has no hash.

options.text: It stores two keys, VOD and BP
options.why: Python does not unpack a list into several keys. It refuses the list outright.
`KeyError` is for reading a missing key. This fails before any bucket is chosen.

feedback.correct: Lists cannot be keys. Use the tuple `("VOD", "BP")`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can a list be hashed?

explain.text: A list can change after it is stored, so Python gives it no hash. `held[("VOD", "BP")] = 1` works, because a tuple cannot change.

quiz.prose: Use the toy rule from this lesson. Add the letters' places in the alphabet (A = 1 to Z = 26). Divide by 5 and keep the remainder.
quiz.question: Which bucket does BARC go in?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add B, A, R and C, then take the remainder after dividing by 5.

byKey.sum: 24 is the letter sum. The bucket is its remainder after dividing by 5.
byKey.quotient: You wrote how many times 5 fits into 24, rounded. The bucket is what is left over: 4.

explain.text: B = 2, A = 1, R = 18 and C = 3 add to 24. Dividing by 5 leaves 4, so BARC goes in bucket 4.

quiz.prose: `a` and `b` are lists of $n$ trade ids each.
quiz.question: Which line finds the ids in both in $O(n)$ on average?

options.text: `common = [x for x in a if x in b]`
options.why: `x in b` scans the list `b` for every `x`, so this is $O(n^2)$.

options.text: `common = [x for x in a if x in sorted(b)]`
options.why: This sorts `b` again for every `x`, and then scans it: worse than $O(n^2)$.

options.text: `common = [x for x in a for y in b if x == y]`
options.why: That compares every pair: $n \times n$ comparisons.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which version hashes the ids instead of scanning a list?

explain.text: Building each set is $O(n)$, and `&` checks each id of one set in the other at $O(1)$ on average. The list versions scan `b` once per `x`, which is $O(n^2)$.
